case_info.scenario: A 31-year-old previously healthy woman was referred to the uveitis service for evaluation of acute unilateral anterior uveitis with hypopyon and an iris lesion. She reported 1 day of right eye pain and blurred vision, without photopsia or floaters. She had started hourly topical prednisolone acetate, 1%, 24 hours prior to presentation without improvement. Uncorrected visual acuity (VA) was 20/50 (pinhole 20/40) OD and 20/20 OS. Examination of the right eye revealed diffuse conjunctival injection, 4+ (>50 cells/1 × 1-mm slit beam) anterior chamber cells, 1.2-mm layered hypopyon, and an iris lesion (Figure 1). The anterior segment of the left eye was unremarkable. Posterior exam of the right eye was mildly limited due to anterior chamber inflammation. There were no obvious vitreous cells in either eye. The left eye had normal anterior segment but showed retinal hemorrhages. Further history revealed systemic symptoms—headache, fatigue, subjective fevers, and left foot erythema—that began 4 days prior. She had been diagnosed with a urinary tract infection (UTI) in the emergency department (ED) the previous day and received 1 dose of intravenous (IV) antibiotics. She denied recreational IV drug use.

case_info.explanation: Acute endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess (secondary to infective endocarditis) D. Perform an anterior chamber tap, administer intravitreal antimicrobials, and transfer to the ED Acute endogenous endophthalmitis is a serious complication of ocular embolic events associated with infective endocarditis. It most frequently involves the retina and choroid due to their rich vascular supply, typically presenting with chorioretinitis, vitreous cells, and haze. Infected emboli may also localize to the ciliary body and iris, causing predominant inflammation in the anterior vitreous and anterior chamber, respectively. Advanced or disseminated cases may evolve into fulminant panuveitis.1 In this patient, the focal white fibrinous iris lesion represented an iris abscess (Figure 1A). Anterior chamber inflammation was pronounced, while the posterior segment was unaffected. Roth spots in the fellow eye (Figure 2), along with fever, recent UTI, and foot cellulitis, suggested infective endocarditis. Reactive arthritis, associated with HLA-B27 in 50% to 75% of cases, may follow a UTI and may present with unilateral uveitis and/or arthritis.2Although HLA-B27 testing (choice A) is valuable to evaluate acute unilateral uveitis with hypopyon, an iris mass lesion is not characteristic. Oral ulcers and fluorescein angiography (choice B) would evaluate for Behçet disease. Behçet uveitis may present with hypopyon and retinal hemorrhages related to retinal vasculitis,3but it is often bilateral and relapsing. Asking about tattoos and ordering chest computed tomography (choice C) may reveal sarcoidosis or tattoo-associated uveitis with iris nodules; however, these rarely present with hypopyon, and iris nodules should be distinguished from abscesses.4,5 Infective endocarditis, most often due to staphylococcal species, may first present with ocular signs.6Risk factors include valve disease, diabetes, poor dentition, recent surgical procedures, and intravenous drug use.6The Modified Duke Criteria incorporate microbiology and clinical features to establish the diagnosis.7Endogenous endophthalmitis may be the initial or sole manifestation of endocarditis, particularly in younger or immunocompetent patients.8 Iris abscesses are uncommon and can be easily missed without careful examination. Reported cases have been linked to intravenous drug use, although this patient denied this risk factor.9 The patient underwent anterior chamber paracentesis with intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime injections. Blood cultures grew methicillin-sensitiveStaphylococcus aureus(MSSA), and aqueous cultures were negative. Echocardiography showed no vegetations or structural abnormalities, except for mild pericardial effusion. Nevertheless, a clinical diagnosis of infective endocarditis was made using the Modified Duke Criteria based on positive blood cultures for MSSA (major criterion), along with fever and immunologic or vascular phenomena, including Roth spots, iris abscess, and cellulitis (minor criteria).7 The patient completed 2 weeks of IV oxacillin and 4 weeks of IV cefazolin. Ocular management included topical moxifloxacin, atropine, and prednisolone acetate. Uncorrected VA recovered to 20/20 both eyes, with mild focal superotemporal iris atrophy in the right eye. She remained recurrence-free at 3 years. This case highlights a presentation of endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess, which may be easily overlooked, as it may not be a widely recognized clinical sign among ophthalmologists. The authors emphasize the importance of careful bilateral anterior and posterior segment evaluation in unilateral uveitis with hypopyon.

Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."

4. Frustration

case_info.explanation: Acute endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess (secondary to infective endocarditis) D. Perform an anterior chamber tap, administer intravitreal antimicrobials, and transfer to the ED Acute endogenous endophthalmitis is a serious complication of ocular embolic events associated with infective endocarditis. It most frequently involves the retina and choroid due to their rich vascular supply, typically presenting with chorioretinitis, vitreous cells, and haze. Infected emboli may also localize to the ciliary body and iris, causing predominant inflammation in the anterior vitreous and anterior chamber, respectively. Advanced or disseminated cases may evolve into fulminant panuveitis.1 In this patient, the focal white fibrinous iris lesion represented an iris abscess (Figure 1A). Anterior chamber inflammation was pronounced, while the posterior segment was unaffected. Roth spots in the fellow eye (Figure 2), along with fever, recent UTI, and foot cellulitis, suggested infective endocarditis. Reactive arthritis, associated with HLA-B27 in 50% to 75% of cases, may follow a UTI and may present with unilateral uveitis and/or arthritis.2Although HLA-B27 testing (choice A) is valuable to evaluate acute unilateral uveitis with hypopyon, an iris mass lesion is not characteristic. Oral ulcers and fluorescein angiography (choice B) would evaluate for Behçet disease. Behçet uveitis may present with hypopyon and retinal hemorrhages related to retinal vasculitis,3but it is often bilateral and relapsing. Asking about tattoos and ordering chest computed tomography (choice C) may reveal sarcoidosis or tattoo-associated uveitis with iris nodules; however, these rarely present with hypopyon, and iris nodules should be distinguished from abscesses.4,5 Infective endocarditis, most often due to staphylococcal species, may first present with ocular signs.6Risk factors include valve disease, diabetes, poor dentition, recent surgical procedures, and intravenous drug use.6The Modified Duke Criteria incorporate microbiology and clinical features to establish the diagnosis.7Endogenous endophthalmitis may be the initial or sole manifestation of endocarditis, particularly in younger or immunocompetent patients.8 Iris abscesses are uncommon and can be easily missed without careful examination. Reported cases have been linked to intravenous drug use, although this patient denied this risk factor.9 The patient underwent anterior chamber paracentesis with intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime injections. Blood cultures grew methicillin-sensitiveStaphylococcus aureus(MSSA), and aqueous cultures were negative. Echocardiography showed no vegetations or structural abnormalities, except for mild pericardial effusion. Nevertheless, a clinical diagnosis of infective endocarditis was made using the Modified Duke Criteria based on positive blood cultures for MSSA (major criterion), along with fever and immunologic or vascular phenomena, including Roth spots, iris abscess, and cellulitis (minor criteria).7 The patient completed 2 weeks of IV oxacillin and 4 weeks of IV cefazolin. Ocular management included topical moxifloxacin, atropine, and prednisolone acetate. Uncorrected VA recovered to 20/20 both eyes, with mild focal superotemporal iris atrophy in the right eye. She remained recurrence-free at 3 years. This case highlights a presentation of endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess, which may be easily overlooked, as it may not be a widely recognized clinical sign among ophthalmologists. The authors emphasize the importance of careful bilateral anterior and posterior segment evaluation in unilateral uveitis with hypopyon.

Perform an anterior chamber tap, administer intravitreal antimicrobials, and transfer to the ED Acute endogenous endophthalmitis is a serious complication of ocular embolic events associated with infective endocarditis. It most frequently involves the retina and choroid due to their rich vascular supply, typically presenting with chorioretinitis, vitreous cells, and haze. Infected emboli may also localize to the ciliary body and iris, causing predominant inflammation in the anterior vitreous and anterior chamber, respectively. Advanced or disseminated cases may evolve into fulminant panuveitis.1 In this patient, the focal white fibrinous iris lesion represented an iris abscess (Figure 1A). Anterior chamber inflammation was pronounced, while the posterior segment was unaffected. Roth spots in the fellow eye (Figure 2), along with fever, recent UTI, and foot cellulitis, suggested infective endocarditis. Reactive arthritis, associated with HLA-B27 in 50% to 75% of cases, may follow a UTI and may present with unilateral uveitis and/or arthritis.2Although HLA-B27 testing (choice A) is valuable to evaluate acute unilateral uveitis with hypopyon, an iris mass lesion is not characteristic. Oral ulcers and fluorescein angiography (choice B) would evaluate for Behçet disease. Behçet uveitis may present with hypopyon and retinal hemorrhages related to retinal vasculitis,3but it is often bilateral and relapsing. Asking about tattoos and ordering chest computed tomography (choice C) may reveal sarcoidosis or tattoo-associated uveitis with iris nodules; however, these rarely present with hypopyon, and iris nodules should be distinguished from abscesses.4,5 Infective endocarditis, most often due to staphylococcal species, may first present with ocular signs.6Risk factors include valve disease, diabetes, poor dentition, recent surgical procedures, and intravenous drug use.6The Modified Duke Criteria incorporate microbiology and clinical features to establish the diagnosis.7Endogenous endophthalmitis may be the initial or sole manifestation of endocarditis, particularly in younger or immunocompetent patients.8 Iris abscesses are uncommon and can be easily missed without careful examination. Reported cases have been linked to intravenous drug use, although this patient denied this risk factor.9 The patient underwent anterior chamber paracentesis with intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime injections. Blood cultures grew methicillin-sensitiveStaphylococcus aureus(MSSA), and aqueous cultures were negative. Echocardiography showed no vegetations or structural abnormalities, except for mild pericardial effusion. Nevertheless, a clinical diagnosis of infective endocarditis was made using the Modified Duke Criteria based on positive blood cultures for MSSA (major criterion), along with fever and immunologic or vascular phenomena, including Roth spots, iris abscess, and cellulitis (minor criteria).7 The patient completed 2 weeks of IV oxacillin and 4 weeks of IV cefazolin. She remained recurrence-free at 3 years. The authors emphasize the importance of careful bilateral anterior and posterior segment evaluation in unilateral uveitis with hypopyon.

   Definition:

   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

   Definition:

     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."

   Definition:

     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."

       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."

   Definition:

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

[Clinical case]
A 31-year-old previously healthy woman was referred to the uveitis service for evaluation of acute unilateral anterior uveitis with hypopyon and an iris lesion. She reported 1 day of right eye pain and blurred vision, without photopsia or floaters. She had started hourly topical prednisolone acetate, 1%, 24 hours prior to presentation without improvement. Uncorrected visual acuity (VA) was 20/50 (pinhole 20/40) OD and 20/20 OS. Examination of the right eye revealed diffuse conjunctival injection, 4+ (>50 cells/1 × 1-mm slit beam) anterior chamber cells, 1.2-mm layered hypopyon, and an iris lesion (Figure 1). The anterior segment of the left eye was unremarkable. Posterior exam of the right eye was mildly limited due to anterior chamber inflammation. There were no obvious vitreous cells in either eye. The left eye had normal anterior segment but showed retinal hemorrhages. Further history revealed systemic symptoms—headache, fatigue, subjective fevers, and left foot erythema—that began 4 days prior. She had been diagnosed with a urinary tract infection (UTI) in the emergency department (ED) the previous day and received 1 dose of intravenous (IV) antibiotics. She denied recreational IV drug use.

case_info.explanation: Acute endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess (secondary to infective endocarditis) D. Perform an anterior chamber tap, administer intravitreal antimicrobials, and transfer to the ED Acute endogenous endophthalmitis is a serious complication of ocular embolic events associated with infective endocarditis. It most frequently involves the retina and choroid due to their rich vascular supply, typically presenting with chorioretinitis, vitreous cells, and haze. Infected emboli may also localize to the ciliary body and iris, causing predominant inflammation in the anterior vitreous and anterior chamber, respectively. Advanced or disseminated cases may evolve into fulminant panuveitis.1 In this patient, the focal white fibrinous iris lesion represented an iris abscess (Figure 1A). Anterior chamber inflammation was pronounced, while the posterior segment was unaffected. Roth spots in the fellow eye (Figure 2), along with fever, recent UTI, and foot cellulitis, suggested infective endocarditis. Reactive arthritis, associated with HLA-B27 in 50% to 75% of cases, may follow a UTI and may present with unilateral uveitis and/or arthritis.2Although HLA-B27 testing (choice A) is valuable to evaluate acute unilateral uveitis with hypopyon, an iris mass lesion is not characteristic. Oral ulcers and fluorescein angiography (choice B) would evaluate for Behçet disease. Behçet uveitis may present with hypopyon and retinal hemorrhages related to retinal vasculitis,3but it is often bilateral and relapsing. Asking about tattoos and ordering chest computed tomography (choice C) may reveal sarcoidosis or tattoo-associated uveitis with iris nodules; however, these rarely present with hypopyon, and iris nodules should be distinguished from abscesses.4,5 Infective endocarditis, most often due to staphylococcal species, may first present with ocular signs.6Risk factors include valve disease, diabetes, poor dentition, recent surgical procedures, and intravenous drug use.6The Modified Duke Criteria incorporate microbiology and clinical features to establish the diagnosis.7Endogenous endophthalmitis may be the initial or sole manifestation of endocarditis, particularly in younger or immunocompetent patients.8 Iris abscesses are uncommon and can be easily missed without careful examination. Reported cases have been linked to intravenous drug use, although this patient denied this risk factor.9 The patient underwent anterior chamber paracentesis with intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime injections. Blood cultures grew methicillin-sensitiveStaphylococcus aureus(MSSA), and aqueous cultures were negative. Echocardiography showed no vegetations or structural abnormalities, except for mild pericardial effusion. Nevertheless, a clinical diagnosis of infective endocarditis was made using the Modified Duke Criteria based on positive blood cultures for MSSA (major criterion), along with fever and immunologic or vascular phenomena, including Roth spots, iris abscess, and cellulitis (minor criteria).7 The patient completed 2 weeks of IV oxacillin and 4 weeks of IV cefazolin. Ocular management included topical moxifloxacin, atropine, and prednisolone acetate. Uncorrected VA recovered to 20/20 both eyes, with mild focal superotemporal iris atrophy in the right eye. She remained recurrence-free at 3 years. This case highlights a presentation of endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess, which may be easily overlooked, as it may not be a widely recognized clinical sign among ophthalmologists. The authors emphasize the importance of careful bilateral anterior and posterior segment evaluation in unilateral uveitis with hypopyon.

case_info.explanation: Acute endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess (secondary to infective endocarditis) D. Perform an anterior chamber tap, administer intravitreal antimicrobials, and transfer to the ED Acute endogenous endophthalmitis is a serious complication of ocular embolic events associated with infective endocarditis. It most frequently involves the retina and choroid due to their rich vascular supply, typically presenting with chorioretinitis, vitreous cells, and haze. Infected emboli may also localize to the ciliary body and iris, causing predominant inflammation in the anterior vitreous and anterior chamber, respectively. Advanced or disseminated cases may evolve into fulminant panuveitis.1 In this patient, the focal white fibrinous iris lesion represented an iris abscess (Figure 1A). Anterior chamber inflammation was pronounced, while the posterior segment was unaffected. Roth spots in the fellow eye (Figure 2), along with fever, recent UTI, and foot cellulitis, suggested infective endocarditis. Reactive arthritis, associated with HLA-B27 in 50% to 75% of cases, may follow a UTI and may present with unilateral uveitis and/or arthritis.2Although HLA-B27 testing (choice A) is valuable to evaluate acute unilateral uveitis with hypopyon, an iris mass lesion is not characteristic. Oral ulcers and fluorescein angiography (choice B) would evaluate for Behçet disease. Behçet uveitis may present with hypopyon and retinal hemorrhages related to retinal vasculitis,3but it is often bilateral and relapsing. Asking about tattoos and ordering chest computed tomography (choice C) may reveal sarcoidosis or tattoo-associated uveitis with iris nodules; however, these rarely present with hypopyon, and iris nodules should be distinguished from abscesses.4,5 Infective endocarditis, most often due to staphylococcal species, may first present with ocular signs.6Risk factors include valve disease, diabetes, poor dentition, recent surgical procedures, and intravenous drug use.6The Modified Duke Criteria incorporate microbiology and clinical features to establish the diagnosis.7Endogenous endophthalmitis may be the initial or sole manifestation of endocarditis, particularly in younger or immunocompetent patients.8 Iris abscesses are uncommon and can be easily missed without careful examination. Reported cases have been linked to intravenous drug use, although this patient denied this risk factor.9 The patient underwent anterior chamber paracentesis with intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime injections. Blood cultures grew methicillin-sensitiveStaphylococcus aureus(MSSA), and aqueous cultures were negative. Echocardiography showed no vegetations or structural abnormalities, except for mild pericardial effusion. Nevertheless, a clinical diagnosis of infective endocarditis was made using the Modified Duke Criteria based on positive blood cultures for MSSA (major criterion), along with fever and immunologic or vascular phenomena, including Roth spots, iris abscess, and cellulitis (minor criteria).7 The patient completed 2 weeks of IV oxacillin and 4 weeks of IV cefazolin. Ocular management included topical moxifloxacin, atropine, and prednisolone acetate. Uncorrected VA recovered to 20/20 both eyes, with mild focal superotemporal iris atrophy in the right eye. She remained recurrence-free at 3 years. This case highlights a presentation of endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess, which may be easily overlooked, as it may not be a widely recognized clinical sign among ophthalmologists. The authors emphasize the importance of careful bilateral anterior and posterior segment evaluation in unilateral uveitis with hypopyon.

case_info.explanation: Acute endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess (secondary to infective endocarditis) D. Perform an anterior chamber tap, administer intravitreal antimicrobials, and transfer to the ED Acute endogenous endophthalmitis is a serious complication of ocular embolic events associated with infective endocarditis. It most frequently involves the retina and choroid due to their rich vascular supply, typically presenting with chorioretinitis, vitreous cells, and haze. Infected emboli may also localize to the ciliary body and iris, causing predominant inflammation in the anterior vitreous and anterior chamber, respectively. Advanced or disseminated cases may evolve into fulminant panuveitis.1 In this patient, the focal white fibrinous iris lesion represented an iris abscess (Figure 1A). Anterior chamber inflammation was pronounced, while the posterior segment was unaffected. Roth spots in the fellow eye (Figure 2), along with fever, recent UTI, and foot cellulitis, suggested infective endocarditis. Reactive arthritis, associated with HLA-B27 in 50% to 75% of cases, may follow a UTI and may present with unilateral uveitis and/or arthritis.2Although HLA-B27 testing (choice A) is valuable to evaluate acute unilateral uveitis with hypopyon, an iris mass lesion is not characteristic. Oral ulcers and fluorescein angiography (choice B) would evaluate for Behçet disease. Behçet uveitis may present with hypopyon and retinal hemorrhages related to retinal vasculitis,3but it is often bilateral and relapsing. Asking about tattoos and ordering chest computed tomography (choice C) may reveal sarcoidosis or tattoo-associated uveitis with iris nodules; however, these rarely present with hypopyon, and iris nodules should be distinguished from abscesses.4,5 Infective endocarditis, most often due to staphylococcal species, may first present with ocular signs.6Risk factors include valve disease, diabetes, poor dentition, recent surgical procedures, and intravenous drug use.6The Modified Duke Criteria incorporate microbiology and clinical features to establish the diagnosis.7Endogenous endophthalmitis may be the initial or sole manifestation of endocarditis, particularly in younger or immunocompetent patients.8 Iris abscesses are uncommon and can be easily missed without careful examination. Reported cases have been linked to intravenous drug use, although this patient denied this risk factor.9 The patient underwent anterior chamber paracentesis with intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime injections. Blood cultures grew methicillin-sensitiveStaphylococcus aureus(MSSA), and aqueous cultures were negative. Echocardiography showed no vegetations or structural abnormalities, except for mild pericardial effusion. Nevertheless, a clinical diagnosis of infective endocarditis was made using the Modified Duke Criteria based on positive blood cultures for MSSA (major criterion), along with fever and immunologic or vascular phenomena, including Roth spots, iris abscess, and cellulitis (minor criteria).7 The patient completed 2 weeks of IV oxacillin and 4 weeks of IV cefazolin. Ocular management included topical moxifloxacin, atropine, and prednisolone acetate. Uncorrected VA recovered to 20/20 both eyes, with mild focal superotemporal iris atrophy in the right eye. She remained recurrence-free at 3 years. This case highlights a presentation of endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess, which may be easily overlooked, as it may not be a widely recognized clinical sign among ophthalmologists. The authors emphasize the importance of careful bilateral anterior and posterior segment evaluation in unilateral uveitis with hypopyon.

A 31-year-old previously healthy woman was referred to the uveitis service for evaluation of acute unilateral anterior uveitis with hypopyon and an iris lesion. Further history revealed systemic symptoms—headache, fatigue, subjective fevers, and left foot erythema—that began 4 days prior. You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

[Deliberation Stage: INFORM]
Discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts relevant to the clinical case.

   Definition:

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.

       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging

       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."

       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:

       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Acute endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess (secondary to infective endocarditis) D. Perform an anterior chamber tap, administer intravitreal antimicrobials, and transfer to the ED Acute endogenous endophthalmitis is a serious complication of ocular embolic events associated with infective endocarditis. It most frequently involves the retina and choroid due to their rich vascular supply, typically presenting with chorioretinitis, vitreous cells, and haze. Infected emboli may also localize to the ciliary body and iris, causing predominant inflammation in the anterior vitreous and anterior chamber, respectively. Advanced or disseminated cases may evolve into fulminant panuveitis.1 In this patient, the focal white fibrinous iris lesion represented an iris abscess (Figure 1A). Anterior chamber inflammation was pronounced, while the posterior segment was unaffected. Roth spots in the fellow eye (Figure 2), along with fever, recent UTI, and foot cellulitis, suggested infective endocarditis. Reactive arthritis, associated with HLA-B27 in 50% to 75% of cases, may follow a UTI and may present with unilateral uveitis and/or arthritis.2Although HLA-B27 testing (choice A) is valuable to evaluate acute unilateral uveitis with hypopyon, an iris mass lesion is not characteristic. Oral ulcers and fluorescein angiography (choice B) would evaluate for Behçet disease. Behçet uveitis may present with hypopyon and retinal hemorrhages related to retinal vasculitis,3but it is often bilateral and relapsing. Asking about tattoos and ordering chest computed tomography (choice C) may reveal sarcoidosis or tattoo-associated uveitis with iris nodules; however, these rarely present with hypopyon, and iris nodules should be distinguished from abscesses.4,5 Infective endocarditis, most often due to staphylococcal species, may first present with ocular signs.6Risk factors include valve disease, diabetes, poor dentition, recent surgical procedures, and intravenous drug use.6The Modified Duke Criteria incorporate microbiology and clinical features to establish the diagnosis.7Endogenous endophthalmitis may be the initial or sole manifestation of endocarditis, particularly in younger or immunocompetent patients.8 Iris abscesses are uncommon and can be easily missed without careful examination. Reported cases have been linked to intravenous drug use, although this patient denied this risk factor.9 The patient underwent anterior chamber paracentesis with intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime injections. Blood cultures grew methicillin-sensitiveStaphylococcus aureus(MSSA), and aqueous cultures were negative. Echocardiography showed no vegetations or structural abnormalities, except for mild pericardial effusion. Nevertheless, a clinical diagnosis of infective endocarditis was made using the Modified Duke Criteria based on positive blood cultures for MSSA (major criterion), along with fever and immunologic or vascular phenomena, including Roth spots, iris abscess, and cellulitis (minor criteria).7 The patient completed 2 weeks of IV oxacillin and 4 weeks of IV cefazolin. Ocular management included topical moxifloxacin, atropine, and prednisolone acetate. Uncorrected VA recovered to 20/20 both eyes, with mild focal superotemporal iris atrophy in the right eye. She remained recurrence-free at 3 years. This case highlights a presentation of endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess, which may be easily overlooked, as it may not be a widely recognized clinical sign among ophthalmologists. The authors emphasize the importance of careful bilateral anterior and posterior segment evaluation in unilateral uveitis with hypopyon.

case_info.explanation: Acute endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess (secondary to infective endocarditis) D. Perform an anterior chamber tap, administer intravitreal antimicrobials, and transfer to the ED Acute endogenous endophthalmitis is a serious complication of ocular embolic events associated with infective endocarditis. It most frequently involves the retina and choroid due to their rich vascular supply, typically presenting with chorioretinitis, vitreous cells, and haze. Infected emboli may also localize to the ciliary body and iris, causing predominant inflammation in the anterior vitreous and anterior chamber, respectively. Advanced or disseminated cases may evolve into fulminant panuveitis.1 In this patient, the focal white fibrinous iris lesion represented an iris abscess (Figure 1A). Anterior chamber inflammation was pronounced, while the posterior segment was unaffected. Roth spots in the fellow eye (Figure 2), along with fever, recent UTI, and foot cellulitis, suggested infective endocarditis. Reactive arthritis, associated with HLA-B27 in 50% to 75% of cases, may follow a UTI and may present with unilateral uveitis and/or arthritis.2Although HLA-B27 testing (choice A) is valuable to evaluate acute unilateral uveitis with hypopyon, an iris mass lesion is not characteristic. Oral ulcers and fluorescein angiography (choice B) would evaluate for Behçet disease. Behçet uveitis may present with hypopyon and retinal hemorrhages related to retinal vasculitis,3but it is often bilateral and relapsing. Asking about tattoos and ordering chest computed tomography (choice C) may reveal sarcoidosis or tattoo-associated uveitis with iris nodules; however, these rarely present with hypopyon, and iris nodules should be distinguished from abscesses.4,5 Infective endocarditis, most often due to staphylococcal species, may first present with ocular signs.6Risk factors include valve disease, diabetes, poor dentition, recent surgical procedures, and intravenous drug use.6The Modified Duke Criteria incorporate microbiology and clinical features to establish the diagnosis.7Endogenous endophthalmitis may be the initial or sole manifestation of endocarditis, particularly in younger or immunocompetent patients.8 Iris abscesses are uncommon and can be easily missed without careful examination. Reported cases have been linked to intravenous drug use, although this patient denied this risk factor.9 The patient underwent anterior chamber paracentesis with intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime injections. Blood cultures grew methicillin-sensitiveStaphylococcus aureus(MSSA), and aqueous cultures were negative. Echocardiography showed no vegetations or structural abnormalities, except for mild pericardial effusion. Nevertheless, a clinical diagnosis of infective endocarditis was made using the Modified Duke Criteria based on positive blood cultures for MSSA (major criterion), along with fever and immunologic or vascular phenomena, including Roth spots, iris abscess, and cellulitis (minor criteria).7 The patient completed 2 weeks of IV oxacillin and 4 weeks of IV cefazolin. Ocular management included topical moxifloxacin, atropine, and prednisolone acetate. Uncorrected VA recovered to 20/20 both eyes, with mild focal superotemporal iris atrophy in the right eye. She remained recurrence-free at 3 years. This case highlights a presentation of endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess, which may be easily overlooked, as it may not be a widely recognized clinical sign among ophthalmologists. The authors emphasize the importance of careful bilateral anterior and posterior segment evaluation in unilateral uveitis with hypopyon.
